objectives.text: Explain the new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus in plain language, linking it to the patient's symptoms, labs, and personal risk factors (prior gestational diabetes, family history).
Initiate metformin appropriately given normal renal function, addressing dosing, titration, and common side effects, while incorporating the patient's fear of injections and cost concerns.

Negotiate realistic, context-specific self-management goals that account for rotating shift work, sweet tea/energy drink intake, skipped meals, and caregiving demands rather than prescribing a generic diet and exercise plan.

Identify and address gaps in diabetes-related preventive care: dilated eye exam referral, in-person comprehensive foot exam referral, immunizations, lipid management, and nephropathy screening/monitoring.

Recognize and sensitively explore the patient-chart mismatch regarding missed postpartum glucose follow-up and the discrepancy between her sense of being on top of things and the record showing a lapse in follow-up.
Screen for psychosocial distress and health literacy barriers (conflicting online information, overwhelm, fear) and respond with targeted education and emotional support within NP scope.

answerKey.primaryProblem: New diagnosis of type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.6%, fasting glucose 178 mg/dL) in a 38-year-old woman with prior gestational diabetes, strong family history, obesity (BMI 34), and acanthosis nigricans, with concurrent hyperlipidemia and a urine albumin-creatinine ratio in the normal (A1) range.
differential: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (confirmed by HbA1c ≥6.5% and fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL on two measures - lab and home log)

Latent autoimmune diabetes in adults (less likely given age, obesity, acanthosis nigricans, and clinical picture consistent with insulin resistance rather than autoimmune beta-cell failure; not routinely tested for in this low-pretest-probability presentation)
Secondary causes of hyperglycemia (e.g., steroid use, Cushing syndrome) - unlikely, no history of exogenous steroid use or clinical features suggestive of Cushing's
Diabetes insipidus - unlikely given hyperglycemia on labs; polyuria/polydipsia explained by osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia
keyFindings: HbA1c 8.6% and fasting glucose 178 mg/dL meet ADA criteria for diabetes diagnosis
Classic osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, fatigue) and recurrent candidal infections consistent with hyperglycemia
Acanthosis nigricans on exam supporting insulin resistance
LDL 142 mg/dL and total cholesterol 218 mg/dL indicate need for lipid management
Urine ACR 22 mg/g is in the A1 category (normal, <30 mg/g); eGFR 98 is normal; routine periodic monitoring is still warranted given new diabetes diagnosis
BMI 34 kg/m^2 (Obesity Class I) is a modifiable risk factor
History of gestational diabetes and strong family history of diabetic nephropathy place her at elevated lifetime risk
Home glucose log confirms persistently elevated fasting values (165-188 mg/dL) over 10 days, corroborating lab findings
plan: Diagnose type 2 diabetes mellitus and explain diagnosis clearly, addressing fear related to mother's dialysis course

Initiate metformin 500 mg orally once daily with evening meal, titrate up gradually (e.g., increase by 500 mg every 1-2 weeks as tolerated) to a target of 1000 mg twice daily, with counseling on GI side effects and taking with food
Confirm renal function supports metformin use (eGFR 98, normal) and plan to recheck renal function periodically
Order repeat fasting lipid panel in 3 months; discuss statin therapy per ASCVD risk given LDL 142 and diabetes diagnosis (shared decision-making, likely moderate-intensity statin indicated)
Refer for dilated eye exam (ophthalmology/optometry) within the next few months given no documented exam in the past year
Refer for an in-person comprehensive diabetic foot exam (monofilament, vibration sense, pulses); this cannot be completed by camera and the visual-only check performed today does not replace it
Repeat urine albumin-creatinine ratio in 3-6 months as routine monitoring given new diabetes diagnosis; reinforce blood pressure control

Set collaborative, shift-work-sensitive goals: reduce sweet tea/energy drink intake, substitute lower-sugar hydration options during shifts, aim to not skip breakfast, consider small protein-containing meal before shift
Recommend brief walking or activity bouts fitted around caregiving/work schedule rather than a generic exercise prescription

Address immunization gaps: offer influenza vaccine, Hepatitis B series (ACIP recommends offering to adults with diabetes aged 19-59; she is 38), update Tdap timing per schedule, COVID-19 booster per current guidance

Screen for diabetes distress and depression (PHQ-9 administered, mild score; validated distress screen administered, moderate distress); offer diabetes self-management education and support (DSME/S) referral
Discuss cost concerns: confirm metformin is low-cost/generic, explore patient assistance or $4 generic programs if needed
Arrange follow-up visit in 4-6 weeks to assess metformin tolerance, titration, and glucose trends; reinforce home glucose monitoring technique and frequency
Note copper IUD is non-hormonal and does not need to be changed; no interaction with metformin
redFlags: Signs of diabetic ketoacidosis (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid breathing) - advise to seek emergency care if these develop
Severe hyperglycemia symptoms (confusion, extreme lethargy) warrant urgent evaluation
Progression of albuminuria into the A2 range (30-300 mg/g) or declining eGFR would need escalation to nephrology referral
Vision changes or eye pain should prompt urgent ophthalmologic evaluation
educationPoints: Type 2 diabetes is manageable and does not automatically mean insulin or dialysis; many people control it long-term with oral medication and lifestyle changes
Metformin is a first-line, generally well-tolerated, inexpensive medication; GI upset is common early on and often improves by taking with food and titrating slowly
Small, sustainable changes (swapping some sweet tea for water or diet options, not skipping breakfast) are more realistic and effective long-term than drastic diet overhauls
Prior gestational diabetes significantly raises lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes, which is why postpartum and periodic screening is recommended
Family history of diabetic complications does not predetermine her outcome; consistent follow-up and early treatment reduce risk of complications
Online health information varies widely in quality; patient is encouraged to bring questions from her research to her care team to verify
Routine eye exams, foot checks, kidney monitoring, and vaccinations are part of comprehensive diabetes care, not signs that things are worse than they seem

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient believes she has been reasonably on top of her health follow-up, mentioning she 'meant to come back sooner' but frames the delay as minor.
mismatches.recordEvidence: OB/GYN discharge summary from 4 years ago explicitly recommended postpartum glucose testing at 6-12 weeks and periodic diabetes screening given her gestational diabetes history; no documentation exists in the chart that this postpartum testing or periodic screening ever occurred until the current labs were drawn.
mismatches.teachingPoint: Patients may underestimate gaps in preventive follow-up; the clinician should gently surface this using the record rather than assuming full self-report accuracy, and use it to reinforce the importance of consistent follow-up going forward without shaming the patient.

mismatches.patientClaim: Patient reports her home fasting glucose readings have been 'in the 160s to high 180s' over the past week and a half, described verbally as a general range.
mismatches.recordEvidence: The actual home glucose log trend chart shows specific daily values ranging from 165 to 188 mg/dL across 10 days, all consistently above the normal fasting range of 70-99 mg/dL, confirming her verbal report is accurate but allowing the clinician to review the precise pattern and variability.
mismatches.teachingPoint: When a patient-reported trend is available as a logged artifact, reviewing the actual data (rather than relying solely on verbal recall) allows the clinician to assess patterns, variability, and timing that inform medication titration decisions.

patient.name: Shanelle Robinson
patient.appearance: A woman in her late 30s with shoulder-length braided hair, wearing a work polo shirt, seated at a kitchen table with a child's artwork visible taped to the wall behind her. She appears tired, with slightly furrowed brows, and glances occasionally toward the hallway as if listening for her kids; her affect is engaged but visibly anxious when discussing her mother.

persona.personality: Practical, hardworking, and protective of her children; carries herself with quiet strength but is emotionally guarded about her own health needs.
persona.communicationStyle: Direct and conversational, uses everyday language, sometimes talks quickly when anxious, appreciates when things are explained simply without being talked down to.
persona.emotionalState: Anxious and overwhelmed beneath a composed exterior, especially when the conversation turns to her mother's dialysis; motivated once she feels heard and given a concrete plan.
persona.background: Shanelle has worked at the same call center for nine years, moving up to a supervisor role that requires rotating 12-hour shifts. She is raising three children, ages 6, 11, and 15, largely on her own, and her days are organized around their school schedules, her shifts, and keeping the household running. She grew up watching her mother manage diabetes and now dialysis, which shapes much of how she thinks about her own health.
speechExamples: I just want to know what's actually wrong with me, in plain words.
I'm not trying to end up like my mom, hooked up to a machine three times a week.
Between work and the kids, I don't have a lot of room to add one more thing to my plate.
Everybody online says something different and it's honestly kind of confusing.
If it's gonna cost a lot of money, I need to know that upfront.
concerns: Fear of eventually needing insulin injections like her mother
Fear of developing kidney failure and ending up on dialysis
Uncertainty about which online diet/health advice to trust
Cost of new medications on a tight budget
Finding time for self-care given rotating shifts and single parenting

case.title: New Type 2 Diabetes Diagnosis in a 38-Year-Old with Prior Gestational Diabetes
case.summary: Shanelle Robinson, a 38-year-old call-center supervisor and mother of three, returns for a telehealth visit to review labs showing HbA1c 8.6%, fasting glucose 178 mg/dL, LDL 142 mg/dL, and mildly elevated urine ACR, confirming new type 2 diabetes. The case emphasizes patient-centered diagnosis communication, metformin initiation within NP scope, realistic goal-setting around shift work and family demands, and closing preventive care gaps, while addressing her fear of her mother's dialysis course and distress from conflicting online advice.
case.setting: Telehealth video visit, patient at home in her kitchen in Charlotte, NC, during a break between shifts
case.encounterType: Chronic disease management / new diagnosis follow-up
